questions.q: Napoleon suffered his final defeat in 1815 at the Battle of
questions.explanation: Napoleon was defeated at Waterloo in 1815 by an alliance of European powers.

questions.q: Which of these was a multi-ethnic empire in nineteenth-century Europe?
questions.explanation: The Habsburg Empire included Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Italians, Poles and others under one ruler.

questions.q: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Belgium was joined with
questions.explanation: The Kingdom of the Netherlands was set up on France’s northern border, and included Belgium.

questions.q: In the allegory of Germania, the crown of oak leaves stood for
questions.explanation: The oak symbolised heroism, and Germania’s crown of oak leaves showed the German nation’s courage.

questions.q: Why were conservative regimes unable to stop the spread of nationalism after 1815?
options: Ideas of liberty and the nation had already spread among the educated middle classes and could not be easily suppressed
questions.explanation: Repression could not erase ideas that had taken hold among the middle classes and young people.

questions.q: Why did Napoleonic rule lose support in the territories he conquered?
options: Higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription into the French army made it unpopular
questions.explanation: Although the reforms were welcomed at first, the burdens of taxes, censorship and military service turned people against French rule.

questions.q: What were the main ideas of liberalism in the early nineteenth century?
questions.answer: Liberalism stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. Politically it meant government by consent through a constitution and representative assembly, and economically it meant freedom of markets and an end to state restrictions.
keyPoints: Individual freedom and equality before the law
Government by consent with a constitution
questions.explanation: Liberal ideas were mainly supported by the educated middle classes.

questions.q: How did the revolutions of 1848 show both the achievements and the limits of liberal nationalism?
questions.answer: Liberals demanded constitutions and national unity, and conservative rulers made some concessions, such as abolishing serfdom and bonded labour in some areas. But the Frankfurt Parliament failed, monarchs and the army regained control, and women’s demands for the vote were rejected.
keyPoints: Some concessions such as abolition of serfdom
Failure of the Frankfurt Parliament and return of conservative control
questions.explanation: The revolutions did not establish nation-states then, but they left a legacy of ideas.

questions.q: In which year was the Quit India Movement launched?
questions.explanation: The Quit India Movement was launched in August 1942.

questions.q: Dandi, where Gandhiji broke the salt law, is in the state of
questions.explanation: Dandi is a coastal village in Gujarat.

questions.q: Alluri Sitaram Raju led a tribal movement in the
questions.explanation: Raju led a guerrilla-style movement in the Gudem hills against restrictions on forest use.

questions.q: Under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 1931, Gandhiji agreed to
options: attend the Round Table Conference in London and call off the Civil Disobedience Movement
take charge of the British army
questions.explanation: The government agreed to release political prisoners, and Gandhiji took part in the Second Round Table Conference.

questions.q: Why did boycott of mill-made foreign cloth spread slowly among poorer people during Non-Cooperation?
options: Khadi was more expensive than mill cloth, so poor people could not afford it
questions.explanation: Khadi was costlier than mill cloth, and it was hard for the poor to buy it.

questions.q: Why did peasants of Awadh, led by Baba Ramchandra, protest in 1920?
options: Talukdars and landlords demanded high rents and other dues and forced them to work without pay
They wanted to join the army
questions.explanation: The peasants demanded a reduction of revenue, an end to forced labour and social boycott of oppressive landlords.

questions.q: Why was the Simon Commission sent to India in 1927?
questions.answer: It was set up to review the working of the constitutional system under the Government of India Act of 1919 and to suggest changes. All its members were British, so Indians were angry and boycotted it.
questions.explanation: The exclusion of Indians made it unacceptable.

questions.q: How was the Civil Disobedience Movement different from the Non-Cooperation Movement?
questions.answer: In Non-Cooperation people refused to cooperate with the British by boycotting institutions. In Civil Disobedience people were asked not only to refuse cooperation but also to break colonial laws, such as making salt, and to refuse to pay taxes.
keyPoints: Salt law broken; refusal to pay taxes
questions.explanation: Civil Disobedience was a more active form of defiance.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: In which year did Christopher Columbus reach the Americas?
questions.explanation: Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which of these crops is native to the Americas?
questions.explanation: Tomato, potato and maize came to the rest of the world from the Americas.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Why did smallpox cause such huge deaths among the people of the Americas after European arrival?
options: It was spread by animals only
They had no immunity to a disease brought by Europeans
questions.explanation: Native Americans had no immunity to diseases such as smallpox, which helped Europeans conquer them.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which development made it possible to carry fresh meat from distant lands to Europe in the late nineteenth century?
questions.explanation: Refrigerated ships allowed perishable food to be transported over long distances.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Why did assembly-line production make cars cheaper?
options: Mass production reduced the cost per car, making cars affordable for more buyers
questions.explanation: Producing in large numbers with a standard process cut costs.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Why did decolonisation not immediately bring economic freedom to many new countries?
options: They were left with poverty and weak industries and still depended heavily on exporting raw materials
questions.explanation: Colonial rule had left them poor and dependent, so economic development remained a major challenge.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How were many indentured workers recruited, and what were the conditions on arrival?
questions.answer: Agents recruited workers in villages, often giving false information about the work and destination. On arrival, many found harsh living and working conditions, low pay and few rights, and could not easily leave.
keyPoints: Recruited by agents with false promises
Few rights and hard to leave
questions.explanation: Many indentured workers were exploited.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did the abolition of the Corn Laws change British agriculture and world food trade?
questions.answer: Cheap grain was imported from America and eastern Europe, so food prices in Britain fell and many farmers could not compete, and some land went out of cultivation. This stimulated agriculture in other lands, and food began to be traded across the world.
keyPoints: Expansion of agriculture and food trade elsewhere
questions.explanation: The change linked food production in distant regions to British demand.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Which English city was a famous centre of cotton textile manufacturing in the nineteenth century?
questions.explanation: Manchester and the surrounding region of Lancashire had many cotton mills.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Which Indian business family set up the first large iron and steel works at Jamshedpur?
questions.explanation: Jamsetji Tata’s family established the iron and steel company at Jamshedpur.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: In the proto-industrial system, merchants usually
options: gave raw material and advances to peasant families who produced goods at home
questions.explanation: Rural households worked for merchants and were paid for each piece.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did wealthy people in Victorian Britain often prefer handmade goods?
options: Handmade goods symbolised refinement and class
questions.explanation: Aristocrats and the bourgeoisie saw handmade goods as finer than mass-produced ones.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did raw cotton prices rise in India in the 1860s?
options: Cotton had gone out of fashion
The American Civil War cut off cotton supplies to Britain, which then bought more from India
questions.explanation: As Britain turned to India for cotton, prices rose and Indian weavers found it hard to buy cotton.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did the number of workers in Indian mills vary through the year?
options: Mills were closed every summer by law
Many workers were migrants from villages who went back home for the harvest and for festivals
Workers had no need for jobs
questions.explanation: Many mill workers kept links with their villages and left for farm work and festivals.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: How did advertisements help to create new consumers in the nineteenth century?
questions.answer: Advertisements in newspapers, hoardings, labels and calendars made products visible and desirable, and they helped to persuade people to try new goods and to create new needs among consumers.
keyPoints: Made products visible through newspapers, labels and calendars
Persuaded people to buy new goods
questions.explanation: Advertising shaped consumption habits.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Describe two ways in which industrialisation changed the cities of Britain.
questions.answer: Cities grew rapidly as people migrated to work in factories, which led to overcrowded housing, poor sanitation and pollution. New factories, railways and workers’ districts changed the look of towns.
questions.explanation: Urban growth was fast and often unplanned.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Who brought knowledge of woodblock printing from China to Italy?
questions.explanation: Marco Polo, the Italian traveller, returned from China with knowledge of woodblock printing.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Premchand is a well-known writer of
questions.explanation: Premchand’s Hindi fiction is considered a landmark of modern Hindi literature.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: The novels of Charles Dickens often depicted
options: the lives of the poor in Victorian England
questions.explanation: Dickens wrote about poverty, factories and city life in Victorian England.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Menocchio, the miller from Italy, was punished by the Church because
options: his reading led him to ideas about God and the world that the Church considered heretical
questions.explanation: He was prosecuted by the Church for unorthodox ideas that he formed from reading books.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did print help religious and social reform debates in colonial India?
options: It was used only by the British
Printed tracts and newspapers let reformers and their opponents argue in public and reach a wider audience
questions.explanation: Print carried competing views to large audiences, which made public debate possible.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Why was the use of faster printing machines and cheaper paper important in the nineteenth century?
options: They made print cheaper and quicker, so newspapers and books reached mass audiences
questions.explanation: Mass printing gave newspapers and books a far bigger readership.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Mention two ways in which print helped spread knowledge in Europe.
questions.answer: Books could be produced in large numbers and cheaply, so more people could read them. Printed Bibles, pamphlets and newspapers carried new ideas to ordinary readers and encouraged reading and debate.
keyPoints: Books produced cheaply and in large numbers
questions.explanation: Print widened access to knowledge.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did print change the role of women as readers and writers in nineteenth-century Europe?
questions.answer: More women became readers because of cheaper books and lending libraries, and some became writers. Novelists such as Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters and George Eliot showed new images of women.
keyPoints: Women writers such as Jane Austen
questions.explanation: Print opened new opportunities for women.

questions.q: Which of the following is a biotic resource?
questions.explanation: Biotic resources come from the biosphere and have life, such as fish, plants and animals.

questions.q: Wind energy is an example of a
questions.explanation: Wind is continuously replenished, so it is renewable.

questions.q: Which soil is most suitable for crops such as wheat, rice and sugarcane?
questions.explanation: Alluvial soil is fertile and well suited to many crops.

questions.q: Laterite soil is mostly suitable for crops such as
questions.explanation: With added manure and fertiliser, laterite soils suit tea, coffee and cashew.

questions.q: Why is gully erosion a serious problem?
options: Running water cuts deep channels in the soil, making land unfit for cultivation
It happens only in the desert
questions.explanation: Gullies deepen into ravines and render land unfit for farming, as in the Chambal region.

questions.q: Why does the indiscriminate use of resources create social problems?
options: It has no effect on society
Resources get concentrated in a few hands, dividing society into rich and poor
questions.explanation: Unequal access to scarce resources increases inequality and conflict.

questions.q: Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Renewable resources can be replaced or renewed naturally, such as solar and wind energy, water and forests. Non-renewable resources occur over millions of years and cannot be replaced quickly once used, such as coal, petroleum and minerals.
keyPoints: Renewable: can be replenished, e.g. wind, water
Non-renewable: take millions of years, e.g. coal, petroleum
questions.explanation: The difference is the rate of replenishment.

questions.q: Why is Agenda 21 relevant to resource planning at the local level?
questions.answer: Agenda 21 asks every local government to draw up its own local Agenda 21, so that communities plan the sustainable use of resources and the protection of the environment in their own area.
keyPoints: Local governments prepare their own plans
questions.explanation: Local action is needed to achieve global sustainability goals.

questions.q: Coffee in India is mainly grown in
questions.explanation: Karnataka is the leading coffee-producing state.

questions.q: Which of these is an oilseed crop?
questions.explanation: Groundnut is an important oilseed; others include mustard and sesamum.

questions.q: Ragi, a millet, is particularly rich in
questions.explanation: Ragi is a nutritious millet with high iron and calcium content.

questions.q: Rabi crops are harvested in
questions.explanation: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in summer.

questions.q: Why is irrigation important in a monsoon country like India?
options: It replaces rain in all places and times
It is harmful for every crop
Rainfall is uncertain and unevenly distributed, so irrigation helps to protect crops in dry spells
questions.explanation: Rain falls in a few months and varies from year to year, so irrigation secures crops.

questions.q: Why is crop rotation useful for farmers?
options: Growing different crops in turn helps to keep soil fertile and reduces pests
questions.explanation: Different crops use and return different nutrients, and rotation breaks pest cycles.

questions.q: List three features of plantation agriculture.
questions.answer: It is practised on large estates, usually a single crop is grown, much capital and labour is used, and the produce is sold in markets, often exported. Tea, coffee, rubber and sugarcane are examples.
questions.explanation: Plantation farming is commercial farming on a large scale.

questions.q: Why are river valley projects called multipurpose? Mention three purposes.
questions.answer: They serve several purposes at once: irrigation, generation of hydroelectricity, flood control, water supply for homes and industry, inland navigation and fish breeding.
questions.explanation: One dam can provide many benefits.

questions.q: Hydroelectricity is produced using the force of
questions.explanation: Falling water turns turbines to generate hydroelectric power.

questions.q: Biogas is produced from
options: organic waste such as cattle dung
questions.explanation: Biogas is made by the decomposition of organic waste such as dung and crop residues.

questions.q: The Bhilai steel plant is located in
questions.explanation: Bhilai is in Chhattisgarh.

questions.q: Besides limestone, silica and alumina, the cement industry also needs
questions.explanation: Gypsum is used in cement, and limestone is the main raw material.

questions.q: Why are aluminium smelting plants located near sources of cheap electricity?
options: They need huge amounts of electricity, so cheap power lowers costs
They are located only in cities
Electricity is not used in smelting
questions.explanation: Smelting aluminium consumes large amounts of electricity.

questions.q: Why do thermal power stations raise environmental concerns?
options: Burning coal releases carbon dioxide and ash that pollute the air
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels pollutes air and adds greenhouse gases.

questions.q: What is the difference between agro-based and mineral-based industries? Give two examples of each.
questions.answer: Agro-based industries use raw material from agriculture, such as cotton textiles, sugar and jute. Mineral-based industries use minerals as raw material, such as iron and steel, cement and aluminium.
keyPoints: Agro-based use farm products, e.g. cotton, sugar
Mineral-based use minerals, e.g. iron and steel, cement
questions.explanation: Industries are classified by their raw material.

questions.q: Why is it essential to conserve energy? Suggest three ways of doing so.
questions.answer: Sources of energy such as coal and oil are limited and burning them pollutes the environment, so saving energy is important. We can use public transport, switch off unused appliances, use energy-efficient devices and prefer renewable sources.
keyPoints: Energy sources are limited and polluting
Switch off unused appliances or use efficient devices
questions.explanation: Saving energy conserves resources and reduces pollution.

questions.q: The Panchayati Raj system was given constitutional status by an amendment passed in
questions.explanation: The 73rd Amendment of 1992 made panchayats constitutional bodies.

questions.q: Chandigarh and Lakshadweep are examples of
questions.explanation: Union Territories are too small to be states and are administered by the Centre.

questions.q: Which of these subjects is in the State List?
questions.explanation: Police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation are State List subjects.

questions.q: In Belgium, the capital Brussels has
options: a separate government in which both communities have equal representation
questions.explanation: This arrangement was made to ensure fairness to the Dutch-speaking minority in Brussels.

questions.q: How does a federal system differ from a unitary system?
options: A unitary system has several levels of independent governments
A federation has only one government
In a federation power is divided between levels with constitutional guarantee, while in a unitary system the central government can give orders to provincial ones
questions.explanation: In a unitary system the central government is supreme, whereas in a federation the powers of each level are guaranteed.

questions.q: Why is power sharing considered a ‘moral’ reason in a democracy?
options: It is the very spirit of democracy, which means people have a right to be consulted on how they are governed
questions.explanation: Democracy means that people rule themselves, so power should be shared with them.

questions.q: Explain the term ‘majoritarianism’.
questions.answer: Majoritarianism is the belief that the majority community should be able to rule a country in whatever way it wants, even at the cost of the minority. Sri Lanka’s treatment of its Tamil minority is an example.
questions.explanation: It is opposite to the principle of power sharing.

questions.q: How has coalition politics since 1990 changed the working of federalism in India?
questions.answer: Regional parties have become partners in national coalitions, so the Union government has to respect the views of the states. The Supreme Court has also limited the arbitrary dismissal of state governments, which has strengthened federalism.
keyPoints: Regional parties are partners in governments
Limits on dismissal of state governments
questions.explanation: Sharing power at the Centre strengthened the position of states.

questions.q: Members of the Lok Sabha are
questions.explanation: Lok Sabha members are directly elected by voters.

questions.q: Election symbols are allotted to political parties and candidates by the
questions.explanation: The Election Commission allots symbols so that voters, including those who cannot read, can identify them.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of dictatorship?
options: Citizens have no right to choose or remove rulers
questions.explanation: In a dictatorship, rulers are not chosen by the people and cannot be removed by them.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Fundamental Right in India?
questions.explanation: The Right to Equality is one of the Fundamental Rights.

questions.q: Why is competition among parties good for democracy?
options: It makes sure no one votes
It keeps governments alert to people’s needs and gives voters a choice
questions.explanation: Competition forces parties to listen to voters and offer programmes.

questions.q: Why is the growing role of money in elections a challenge to democracy?
options: It lowers the cost of elections
It gives rich candidates and parties an unfair advantage and can keep ordinary citizens out
questions.explanation: Heavy spending distorts competition and favours the wealthy.

questions.q: What is meant by universal adult franchise?
questions.answer: It is the principle that every adult citizen, above the minimum age, has the right to vote regardless of caste, religion, gender, education or wealth. Each person has one vote and each vote has equal value.
keyPoints: No discrimination on caste, religion, gender, wealth
questions.explanation: Equal voting rights are the basis of democratic elections.

questions.q: Why is a democratic government better than a dictatorship at handling conflicts?
questions.answer: In a democracy different groups can voice their demands, negotiate and settle disputes through discussion, elections and courts. A dictatorship suppresses disagreement, so conflicts can grow and may end in violence.
keyPoints: Democracy allows negotiation and peaceful settlement
questions.explanation: Democracy provides peaceful means to resolve differences.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Which of these is a secondary sector activity?
questions.explanation: Turning sugarcane into sugar is manufacturing, a secondary activity.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: The Net Attendance Ratio shows
options: the percentage of children in an age group who attend school
the number of teachers in a state
the number of schools in a district
the number of books in a library
questions.explanation: It is the number of children in an age group attending school as a percentage of all children in that age group.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Which of these is an example of seasonal unemployment?
options: A government clerk with a permanent job
Workers in a sugar factory who find work only in the crushing season
questions.explanation: Seasonal unemployment occurs when work is available only during certain months.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Which of these is an example of the unorganised sector?
questions.explanation: Street vendors work without registration, fixed wages or job security.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: What does the fact that agriculture contributes a smaller share of GDP than its share of employment suggest?
options: A large number of people depend on a sector that produces a smaller share of income, showing low productivity or underemployment
questions.explanation: Many workers share a smaller income pie, so average earnings are low.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why is employment in the services sector not equally good for all workers?
options: Some services such as IT and banking pay well, but many others, like small shops and casual work, are low-paid and insecure
All services pay very high wages
All service workers have permanent jobs
questions.explanation: The tertiary sector contains both well-paid and poorly paid jobs.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Name the three sectors of the economy and give one example of each.
questions.answer: The primary sector uses natural resources, as in agriculture or mining. The secondary sector manufactures goods, as in making cloth or steel. The tertiary sector provides services, as in transport or banking.
questions.explanation: Sectors are classified by the nature of the activity.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why is the public sector needed even when private companies exist?
questions.answer: The government provides things that private firms may not, such as roads, irrigation, schools, hospitals and cheap food through the public distribution system, because they are essential and cannot be left to profit-seeking firms alone.
keyPoints: Private firms may not serve the poor
questions.explanation: Public provision ensures essential services reach everyone.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: The amount a borrower pays to a lender above the sum borrowed is called
questions.explanation: Interest is the price paid for using borrowed money.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Which of these is a formal source of credit?
questions.explanation: Banks and cooperatives are formal sources supervised by the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: A Self Help Group usually consists of
options: 15 to 20 members, mostly women from the same neighbourhood
questions.explanation: Members meet regularly, save money and give small loans from their pooled savings.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: A tax levied on imported goods is called a
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports, which makes them costlier.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why do governments sometimes place limits on imports?
options: To protect domestic producers from foreign competition
questions.explanation: Trade barriers shield local producers while they develop.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why did the Indian government liberalise foreign trade and investment from 1991?
options: To encourage competition, foreign investment and technology and improve efficiency
questions.explanation: Liberalisation aimed to increase competition and bring in investment and technology.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why is a system of money better than barter?
questions.answer: In barter, trade needs a double coincidence of wants, which is rare. Money removes this difficulty because it is accepted in exchange for any good or service, and so makes trade simpler.
keyPoints: Barter needs double coincidence of wants
questions.explanation: Money acts as a medium of exchange.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: What can a consumer do on receiving a defective product, and why is consumer awareness important?
questions.answer: A consumer can complain to the seller, and if not satisfied approach the District, State or National consumer commission with proof of purchase. Awareness of rights helps people avoid being cheated and take action.
questions.explanation: Informed consumers can seek redress.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a nation-state?
options: A state ruled by foreign emperors
A group of tribes without government
A state in which most citizens share a common identity and history
questions.explanation: In a nation-state, citizens see themselves as sharing a common identity.

questions.q: Which leader is associated with the slogan ‘Swaraj is my birthright’?
questions.explanation: The slogan is associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Second World War ended in
questions.explanation: It began in 1939 and ended in 1945.

questions.q: Kharif crops are sown
options: in June–July with the onset of the monsoon
questions.explanation: Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon and harvested in September–October.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Per capita income is also called
questions.explanation: Per capita income is the average income of a person in a country.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: The ISI mark on a product indicates that it
options: meets quality standards set for industrial and consumer goods
questions.explanation: ISI is a certification mark for the quality of industrial products.

questions.q: Why is agriculture important for the Indian economy?
questions.answer: A large share of the population depends on agriculture for a living, it supplies food for the people and raw material for industries such as cotton and jute, and agricultural products are also exported.
questions.explanation: Agriculture supports livelihoods and industry.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: What is the role of the Reserve Bank of India in the credit system?
questions.answer: The Reserve Bank supervises banks, making sure they maintain cash reserves and give loans not only to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators, small industries and small borrowers, and it also issues currency.
questions.explanation: The RBI oversees the formal banking system.
